title: logo_generation code
text:
Use this space to generate hexagonal stickers for the project. The stickers require the “hexSticker” package so make sure it is installed and loaded. This code requires an external image and can be adjusted accordingly within the shape. It is also possible to use code to create the visualization to be enclosed.

library(ggplot2)
library(hexSticker)


# Install hexSticker if you haven't
# install.packages("hexSticker")

library(hexSticker)

# Create a hex sticker with an image of your choosing
sticker(
  subplot = "logo.png",   # Replace with your image path
  s_x = 1, s_y = 1,              # Centering
  s_width = .58, s_height = .58, # Size of the image inside hex
  package = "",          # Text at the bottom
  p_size = 6,
  p_color = "grey20",
  h_fill = "white",             # Background color of the hex
  h_color = "#4A5568",
  h_size=.9,                     # Border color
  filename = "hex_sticker.png"  # Output filename
)

title: Lab 2: Descriptive Statistics - Central Tendency & Data Visualization
text:
A psychology research team is studying student well-being during exam week. They recruited 24 undergraduate students and recorded each participant’s self-reported sleep from the prior night, test-anxiety score, performance on a short memory-recall task, and primary coping strategy.
The team’s research question is:

During exam week, what are the typical levels of sleep, test anxiety, and memory recall among undergraduate students, and which coping strategy is most common?

This is a descriptive question. We will use the mean, median, and mode to describe the sample appropriately. We will also use visualizations to help us understand the distributions of the variables. Finally, we will write a concise APA-style paragraph to summarize the results.

Learning Objectives
By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

Perform simple transformations on continuous variables and explain the effect of these transformations on measures of central tendency.

text: Part B — Analyzing Continuous Variables

title: Lab 2: Descriptive Statistics - Central Tendency & Data Visualization
text:
Central Tendency
We want to find the “typical hours of sleep” (a continuous variable) for the sampled students by finding the Mean, Mode, and Median using SPSS. Follow the following steps:

Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Frequencies.
Move Sleep_Hours_Prior_Night to the Variable(s) box. Check the Display frequency tables box.
Click Statistics, and check boxes for Mean, Median, and Mode
Click Continue, then OK.

The output should show both the frequency table and the three measures of central tendency for Sleep_Hours_Prior_Night.






Checkpoint




Report the three measures of center.
Which of the three measures is the most reliable and why?




Visualizing Continuous Variables (Sleep Hours)
To visualize the distribution of a continuous variable such as sleep_hours, a histogram is one of the most reliable tools. Follow the following steps to create a histogram in SPSS:

Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Frequencies.
Move Sleep_Hours_Prior_Night to the Variable(s) box.
Click Charts, select Histograms, and check Display normal curve.
Click Continue, then OK. Keep the histogram in your output.







Checkpoint



How would you describe the distribution of sleep hours? Is the histogram roughly symmetric, positively skewed, or negatively skewed? The overlayed normal curve can help you determine this.


Another tool that can be used to visualize the distribution of a continuous variable is a box plot. Follow the following steps to create a box plot for Sleep_Hours_Prior_Night in SPSS:

Graphs > Chart Builder.
Select Boxplot from the gallery, then drag the simple box plot icon to the chart preview area.
Drag Sleep_Hours_Prior_Night to the y-axis and click OK. Keep the box plot in your output.







Checkpoint



How would you describe the distribution of sleep hours based on the box plot?




Extreme Scores
Presence of extreme scores (suspected outliers) can influence central tendency. Change the sleep hours for the last participant (id = 24) to 22 hours. Re-run the analysis for Sleep_Hours_Prior_Night and record the new mean, median, and mode. - How does this change affect these values? In this case, which value is more reliable? - How do the distributions change based on the histogram and box plot?


Simple Transformations on Continuous Variables
Now, imagine the research team revises the anxiety scores by adding 5 points to every participant’s score. We can do this in SPSS as follows:

Transform > Compute Variable.
Under Target Variable, write anxiety_plus_5.
Under Numeric Expression write Test_Anxiety_Score + 5.
Click OK.

Look at the data file and you should see a new variable called anxiety_plus_5.
Run the Mean and median for for Test_Anxiety_Score and anxiety_plus_5.






Checkpoint



How did the mean and median anxiety change after adding 5 to each individual score? State the rule for what happens to the mean and median when the same constant is added to every score.

title: Lab 2: Descriptive Statistics - Central Tendency & Data Visualization
text:
Part C — Analyzing Discrete Variables
In most cases, summary statistics such as the mean and median are not useful for discrete variables measured at the nominal or ordinal level. This is because it doesn’t make mathematical sense to add two categories (e.g Male +Female). For these variables, the mode can be used to tell us the category with the highest representation (frequency). A frequency distribution table can be made to identify this.

Frequency Distribution Table for Discrete Variables
A frequency Distribution table is a straight forward tool that can be used to summarize and organize a discrete nominal variable such as Primary_Coping_Startegy. To make the table in SPSS, follow the following steps:
[Be sure to clear the previous analyses before running this one. For example, disable Histograms]

Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Frequencies.
Move Primary_Coping_Strategy to the Variable(s) box.
Check the Display frequency tables box.
Click OK.



Visualizing Discrete Variables
To visualize a discrete variable such as Primary_Coping_Strategy, a bar chart is one of the most reliable tools. Follow the following steps to create a bar chart in SPSS:

Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Frequencies.
Move Primary_Coping_Strategy to the Variable(s) box.
Click Charts, select Bar charts,

Uncheck the Display frequency tables box.
Click OK.

Keep the bar chart in your output.






Tip



Based on the frequency table and bar chart, which coping strategy was the most common among the sample? Report the mode in words, along with its frequency and percentage.

title: Lab 2: Descriptive Statistics - Central Tendency & Data Visualization
text:
Part D — Analyzing Multiple Variables
Although analyzing variables separately is useful, the complexity of life often require us to look at multiple variables together. For example, we may want to know if students who sleep more hours have lower test anxiety scores. To do this, we can use a scatterplot to visualize the relationship between two continuous variables.
Here is how to create a scatterplot for sleep hours vs test anxiety scores in SPSS:

Graphs > Chart Builder.
Select Scatter/Dot from the gallery, then drag the simple scatter icon to the chart preview area.
Drag Sleep_Hours_Prior_Night to the x-axis and Test_Anxiety_Score to the y-axis. Click OK. Keep the scatterplot in your output.

We may also want to compare the mean test anxiety scores by coping strategy. To do this, we can use a bar chart to visualize the mean test anxiety scores for each coping strategy.

Graphs > Chart Builder.
Select Bar from the gallery, then drag the simple bar icon to the chart preview
Drag Primary_Coping_Strategy to the x-axis and Test_Anxiety_Score to the y-axis. Click OK. By default, SPSS will calculate the mean for each group. Keep the bar chart in your output.







Checkpoint




Based on the scatterplot, is there a relationship between sleep hours and test anxiety scores?
Based on the bar chart, which coping strategy is associated with the lowest mean test anxiety score?
Save your SPSS output file as Lab_2_Output_YourLastName.spv.

title: Lab 2: Descriptive Statistics - Central Tendency & Data Visualization
text:
APA-Style Reporting Tips
APA-style results writing should be accurate, concise, and tied to the research question. Use the statistics you produced in SPSS—not estimates from the graph.

Report the sample size as N when referring to the whole sample.
Report the mean as M and the standard deviation as SD.
Report the median as Mdn when it is the better summary for a skewed distribution.
Report a categorical mode in words, followed by its frequency (n) and percentage when useful.
Round consistently, typically to two decimal places unless your instructor directs otherwise.
Describe the distribution when that explains why you selected the median instead of the mean.


Build your Results Paragraph
Use this template to write a paragraph that answers the research question:

The sample (N = ) reported an average of M = hours of sleep (SD = ; Mdn = ). Participants recalled an average of M = ___ words (SD = ) on the memory task. The modal coping strategy was [strategy] (n = , %). Test-anxiety scores were [roughly symmetric / positively skewed / negatively skewed]; therefore, the [mean / median] was the most appropriate indicator of a typical score (M or Mdn = ). Overall, these results suggest that [one sentence summarizing the sample descriptively without making a causal claim].

Row 1: StudentID

Click the Label cell. Type: Student identifier
Click the Measure cell. Click the dropdown arrow and select Nominal.

Why nominal? An ID number is just a name written as a digit — Student #7 isn’t “more” than Student #3.




Row 2: Major

Name: Major

Values: Click the Values cell, then click the small gray … button that appears on the right side of the cell. A “Value Labels” dialog should open.

Click the + sign to show Value box, and type 1. In the Label box, type Psychology. Click Add.
Value 2, Label Biology. Click Add.

Label: Year in school

1 = Freshman, 2 = Sophomore, 3 = Junior, 4 = Senior (Add after each one, then OK)

Row 4: StudyHours

Decimals: change to 1 (allow one decimal place, e.g., 8.5)
Label: Hours spent studying per week

Why Scale? This is a continuous variable with a meaningful zero (0 hours studied means no studying at all), so it meets the textbook’s definition of a ratio scale. Recall that SPSS collapses interval and ratio into one category named Scale.




Row 5: NetflixHours

Note on SPSS’s Measure column



The textbook describes four scales of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) but SPSS collapses the last two into one “Scale” category.

section: Part 3: Run Your First Output/Data Analyses
text:
Part 3: Run Your First Output/Data Analyses
In this section, you’ll run two basic analyses in SPSS: a frequency table for a nominal variable, and summary statistics for a scale variable. Note that the output will appear in a separate window called the Output Viewer and that this output will have to be saved just like the data file.

Frequency table for a nominal variable

Go to the menu bar and click Analyze → Descriptive Statistics → Frequencies. See below

In the dialog box on the left, click Academic Major, then click the arrow button in the middle to move Academic Major into the Variable(s) box on the right. Make sure the box that says “Display Frequency tables” is checked. See below:

Next, click OK.
The Output Viewer window opens with a table showing how many students fall into each major category, and what percentage each represents.



Visualizing a Nominal (or Ordinal) Variable
The common tools used to visualize the distribution of nominal or ordinal variables are bar graphs or pie charts. To create a bar graph for the variable Major, follow the steps steps below:

Analyze → Descriptive Statistics → Frequencies. In the dialog box, select Academic Major and move it to the Variable(s) box.
Click Charts on the right side of the dialog box. In the new dialog box, select Bar charts and click Continue.
C OK. A bar graph will appear in the Output Viewer. The same procedure can be followed to create a pie chart by selecting Pie charts instead of Bar charts in the Charts dialog box.

It is often helpful to have percentages displayed on the vertical axis instead of the raw frequencies. To do this, select the percentages option under the Frequency Charts pop up box (step 2 above).


Frequency Table for a Scale Variable
We want to create a table that summarizes the variable StudyHours. Follow these steps:

Menu bar: Analyze → Descriptive Statistics → Frequencies. If Academic Major is still on the right box, click on it and click the back arrow to move it back to the left.
Now move StudyHours into the “Variable(s)” box as earlier. Make sure the Display frequency tables box is checked.
Click OK. A frequency table appears in the Output Viewer showing each study hour and the corresponding frequency.







Caution



When working with larger data sets, a frequency table on this kind is not helpful. We can use a grouped frequency table instead. Although the grouped frequency table loses some information, it is easier to read and interpret when we have a large number of unique values.


Although our data set is fairly small (n=10), we can still use it to demonstrate the process of creating a grouped frequency table for StudyHours, we will begin by transforming the variable to create three bins (5-10, 11-15, 16-20) as follows:

Menu bar: tranform → Recode into Different Variable.
Move the Variable StudyHours into the Input Variable → Output Variable box as shown below:

In the Output Variable section under name, write StudyHoursGroup (no spaces). In the Label field, write Study Hours Group (spaces allowed) then click Change.
Next, click Old and New Values. The following window will appear:

Start by checking the box that says Output variables are strings.
In the Old Value section, select Range and type 5 in the first box and 10 in the second box as shown in the screenshot above. In the New Value section, write 5-10.
Click Add.
To create the next bin, enter 11 and 15 as earlier, then write 11-15 under New Value, then click Add. Repeat this for 16-20.
Click Continue to return to the previous window, then click OK.

Take a look at the data window and you should see the new variable you just created called StudyHoursGroup.
To create a frequency table, we follow the steps from earlier:

Analyze → Descriptive Statistics → Frequencies.
Move the variable StudyHoursGroup into the “Variable(s)” box. Make sure the Display frequency tables box is checked. You may want to click on Charts and select None.
Click OK. A frequency table appears in the Output Viewer showing how many students fall into each study hour group.



Visualizing a Scale Variable
There are various graphs that can be used to visualize the distribution of a scale variable. The most common ones are histograms, boxplots, dotplots, and stem-and-leaf plots. Histograms are good for showing the shape of the distribution, boxplots are good for showing the shape of the distributions as well as locations of the median, quartiles, and if there are any outliers.
For this lab, we will creat a histogram to visualize the distribution of StudyHours. Here are the steps:

Menu bar: Analyze → Descriptive Statistics → Frequencies. Move the variable StudyHours into the “Variable(s)” box. Uncheck the box Display frequency tables (we do not need the table).
Click Charts on the right side of the dialog box. In the new dialog box, select Histograms and click Continue.
Click OK. A histogram appears in the Output Viewer showing the distribution of StudyHours.







Checkpoint



Based on the histogram, what can you say about the distribution of the study hours? Is the histogram roughly symmetric, skewed to the left, or skewed to the right?

Part 0: SPSS Interface
Look at the bottom of the SPSS window. You’ll see Data View and Variable View options. See below:

title: Lab 3: Measuring Variability
text:
PART A - Overview
In lecture and in the textbook (Chapter 4, Variability), we learned that variability describes how spread out or clustered together a set of scores is. In this lab, you will use SPSS to generate the four measures of variability covered in the chapter:

the range
the interquartile range (IQR)
the variance
the standard deviation

You will also learn about commonly used tools to visualize data variability of a continuous variable and how to report variability in APA style.

title: Lab 3: Measuring Variability
text:
The Data
A psychologist is interested in understanding reaction time and how much reaction times vary from person to person. To investigate this, the psychologist asked 120 participants to complete a Stroop task, a commonly used task in psychology that measures how quickly people can respond when they encounter conflicting information. The variable Stroop_RT_ms records each participant’s reaction time in milliseconds, with larger values indicating slower responses.
Download the dataset from this link then import it to SPSS. To import the data set, follow these steps:

title: Lab 3: Measuring Variability
text:
Why We Measure Variability
Recall from the reading: if every score in a distribution were identical, variability would be zero. In practice, scores differ from one another, and a good measure of variability tells us two things:

How spread out the scores are — are scores clustered close together or scattered widely?
How well a single score represents the whole distribution — the more variability there is, the less confidence we can place in any one statistic (or sample) as being representative of the group.

The textbook illustrates this with adult heights (low variability, tightly clustered around 70 inches) versus adult weights (much higher variability, spread widely around 170 pounds). Keep this contrast in mind.






Checkpoint



Without opening SPSS, which of the following would you expect to have more variability, and why?

The ages of students in a single 4th-grade classroom.
The ages of visitors at a public shopping mall.

title: Lab 3: Measuring Variability
text:
Part B — The Range
The range is the distance between the largest and smallest score in a distribution:
\[\text{Range} = X_{max} - X_{min}\]
It is the simplest measure of variability, but it is also unreliable because it is based on only the two most extreme scores and ignores everything in between.

Get the Range in SPSS

Click Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Descriptives.
Move Stroop_RT_ms into the Variable(s) box.
Click Options… and check Range, Minimum, and Maximum, then click Continue.
Click OK.

Look at the SPSS Output Viewer. You should see a table listing N, Range, Minimum, and Maximum for Stroop_RT_ms.






Checkpoint




What range does SPSS report for this data set? Confirm it by hand using the formula \(\text{Range} = X_{max} - X_{min}\).
Suppose the quiz score of 32 in the data set were changed to 65, with everything else staying the same. Recompute the range by hand. What happened to the range, and what does this tell you about a weakness of using the range as a measure of variability?




NOTE: Please DO NOT close the output window! You can just click on the main file showing the variables and data when you are ready to continue with the other analyses.

section: Part C — Quartiles and the Interquartile Range (IQR)
text:
Part C — Quartiles and the Interquartile Range (IQR)
Because the range is so sensitive to extreme scores, researchers often prefer the interquartile range, which describes the spread of just the middle 50% of the distribution (between the 25th percentile, \(Q_1\), and the 75th percentile, \(Q_3\)):
\[IQR = Q_3 - Q_1\]
The IQR trims off the top 25% and bottom 25% of scores, so a few unusually high or low scores do not distort it the way they distort the range.

Getting Quartiles in SPSS
There are two common ways to get the IQR in SPSS. Try both so you can see how they relate to one another.
Method A — Frequencies

Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Frequencies.
Move Stroop_RT_ms into the Variable(s) box. (Uncheck “Display frequency tables” if you don’t want the full table.)
Click Statistics…, and under Percentile Values check Quartiles. Click Continue, then OK.
SPSS reports the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles (\(Q_1\), the median, and \(Q_3\)). Use the formula \(IQR = Q_3 - Q_1\) to calculate the \(IQR\).

Method B — Explore

Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Explore.
Move Stroop_RT_ms into the Dependent List.
Under Display, choose Statistics. Click OK.
Look at the Descriptives table — SPSS directly labels a row Interquartile Range.







Checkpoint




What value did SPSS report for \(Q_1\), \(Q_3\) Stroop_RT_ms? What \(IQR\) value did you get by using the formula \(\text{Range}=Q_1 - Q_3\)?
Did Method A and Method B give you exactly the same \(IQR\)? (They may differ slightly — SPSS offers several algorithms for calculating percentiles. This is worth noticing, but don’t worry about resolving the discrepancy for this lab.)
Compare the \(IQR\) to the \(Range\) for this same variable (Stroop_RT_ms). Which value is larger, and why does that make sense?

title: Lab 3: Measuring Variability
section: Part C — Standard Deviation and Variance
text:
Part C — Standard Deviation and Variance
Standard deviation is perhaps the most important and most commonly used measure of variability. Conceptually, it measures the standard (average) distance between each score and the mean. The variance is the average of the squared deviations; the standard deviation is simply the square root of the variance, which brings the measure back into the original units of the data.
Both statistics are built from the sum of squared deviations, or \(SS\). We obtain SS by subtracting the mean from each score, squaring the difference (deviation), the summing all squared deviations. Mathematically, this is abbreviated as;
\[SS = \Sigma(X - \bar{X})^2.\]
Population formulas (use \(\mu\) for the mean and divide by \(N\)). The Greek letter \(\sigma^2\) means population variance while \(\sigma\) means population standard deviation.
\[\sigma^2 = \frac{SS}{N} \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{SS}{N}}\]
Sample formulas (use \(M\) for the mean and divide by \(n - 1\) instead of \(n\)). The notation \(s^2\) means sample variance while \(s\) means sample standard deviation.
\[s^2 = \frac{SS}{n-1} \qquad s = \sqrt{\frac{SS}{n-1}}\]






Why n − 1? Degrees of Freedom



A sample mean is calculated from the sample, which places a restriction on the scores: once you know the mean and all but one score, the last score is no longer free to vary — it is fully determined. Only \(n - 1\) of the \(n\) scores are truly free to vary, so a sample has \(df = n - 1\) degrees of freedom. Dividing \(SS\) by \(n-1\) (rather than \(n\)) slightly increases the resulting value, correcting for the fact that a sample’s variability tends to underestimate the population’s variability. This correction makes sample variance an accurate, unbiased estimator of the population variance.
This is exactly what SPSS’s Descriptives procedure does by default — it always computes the sample formulas (\(n-1\) in the denominator), because SPSS assumes your data are a sample unless you tell it otherwise. Keep this in mind whenever you are working with data that represent an entire population.




Standard Deviation for a Sample
We want to find the standard deviation (and other statistics) for the variable Stroop_RT_ms. By default, SPSS computes the sample standard deviation (i.e., divides the \(SS\) by \(n-1\)).
Follow these steps to find the sample standard deviation for the variable Stroop_RT_ms:

Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Descriptives.
Move Stroop_RT_ms into the variables box, click Options…, and check Mean, Variance and Std. deviation. Click Continue, then OK.







Checkpoint




What sample mean (\(M\)), variance (\(s^2\)), and standard deviation (\(s\)) does SPSS report?
What does the standard deviation tell you about the spread of the Stroop_RT_ms scores?






Comparing Variability by Group (Sex)
Suppose we wanted to answer the question, “Do Stroop_RT_ms scores for females spread out more than Stroop_RT_ms scores for male students?

Go to Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Explore.
Move Stroop_RT_ms into the ‘Dependent List’ box. Move Sex into the ‘Factor List’ box — this tells SPSS to split all output by male vs. female.
Click the ‘Statistics’ button and make sure ‘Descriptives’ is checked (this gives you variance, std deviation, min, max, and range for each group). Select std deviation. Click ‘continue’.







Checkpoint




What sample standard deviation (\(s\)) does SPSS report for each group?
What is a possible explanation for the discrepancy in std deviations? (Note: there can be multiple correct answers here).

title: Lab 3: Measuring Variability
text:
Part D — Visualizing Variability
Numbers alone may not always give you an intuitive feel for variability. Sometimes, graphs can be better tools to communicate the insights. Box plots and histograms are among the commonly used graphs to visualize variability of a continuous variable.

Boxplots in SPSS
To create a boxplot for the variable Stroop_RT_ms, follow these steps: 1. Graphs > Chart Builder 2. From the gallery list, choose Box plots, then drag the simple box plot icon to the chart preview area. Drag Stroop_RT_ms to the y-axis and click OK.
The box itself spans from \(Q_1\) to \(Q_3\) (the IQR), with a line in the middle representing the median. Whiskers extend to the most extreme scores that are not flagged as outliers. Any outliers are indicated with a dot or asterisk beyond the whiskers.


Histograms in SPSS
Create a histogram for Stroop_RT_ms. The steps are similar to those for a box plot. Let your instructor know if you need help with this. Once you have your histogram, you can add a normal curve overlay to help visualize how the distribution compares to a normal distribution.






Checkpoint




Describe the distribution of the Stroop_RT_ms scores. Be sure to talk about outliers, middle 50%, and the median.
Based on your histogram, how would you describe the spread of the Stroop_RT_ms?
How do box plots and histograms differ, and what specific information can be derived exclusively from each?

title: Lab 3: Measuring Variability
text:
Part E — APA-Style Reporting
In journals following the APA style, the standard deviation (abbreviated as SD) and the mean (abbreviated as M) are reported in parentheses after the mean, e.g., \(M = 12.45\), \(SD = 3.70\). For skewed data, the median is reported with the IQR, e.g., \(Mdn = 12.45\), \(IQR = 3.70\).). Here is an example of a paragraph that reports the mean and standard deviation for a hypothetical memory recall test:

Female respondents displayed higher memory recall (M = 12.45, SD = 3.70) than male respondents (M = 10.20, SD = 2.80).

✅ AI tools for labs: You may use AI to find step-by-step procedures for performing certain analyses in SPSS, but be sure to implement them in the software yourself. You will be required to submit your software outputs to demonstrate that you actually performed the analyses. You should not use AI to write the interpretations of your analyses — this part is best done by a human.

You may use these guidelines for citing AI-generated content.

❌ AI tools for narrative: You should not use generative AI tools such as ChatGPT to write narrative on assignments. Interpretation of software output, writing up the project report, among others should be written by a human (YOU). If you want to use these tools to check your grammar, you should feel free to do so but be sure to disclose and cite it accordingly.


If you are unsure if the use of a particular resource complies with the academic honesty policy, please contact your instructor.

Tips for Success
Here are a few basic suggestions for how to succeed in this course:

Keep up with Homework
It is essential that you understand how to solve the assigned homework problems and exercises, and more importantly, how and why the skills and techniques covered in the course are used to solve them. I recommend that you begin working on the homework as soon as possible. Avoid leaving your homework until the last minute or working close to the deadline. Completing the homework on time allows you to receive timely feedback, which will help you better understand the material and perform well in other assessment categories such as exams.


Attend Class Regularly
As noted earlier, attendance is a critical part of your success in this course. You should try to attend every class because it is during class time that we will delve deeper into the course material and practice with applications.


Stay Caught Up
Most concepts in this course build on each other cumulatively and you need to stay on top of the material at every stage. If you are having difficulty, don’t expect that the problem will take care of itself and disappear later. Contact me immediately and discuss the problem.


Collaborate with Peers
Many students benefit from sharing their work with others or by having their work questioned by their peers. You should attempt homework problems ahead of time by yourself and then note down any difficulties/questions that you can discuss with your peers. Even if you have no difficulties, you may still learn different and perhaps more efficient ways of solving the same problem during collaborative work. Below are some of the ways through which you can do this: - Canvas Discussion Forums & One Note Collaboration Space - You can post questions and answer others’ questions here. I encourage you to scan hand-written work (if necessary) and upload it alongside your question so people can see how you are thinking.

Zoom sessions – If you cannot meet in person, you can initiate Zoom sessions for collaborating. Zoom whiteboards are available to write on or you may simply have discussions. You can record these for later playback. If you want to invite me to your Zoom session, please send me an email with the link ahead of time and I will let you know if I am available to join.
